newsitem.title: FRANCE: White House rebukes Gephardt on China trade policy.
newsitem.headline: White House rebukes Gephardt on China trade policy.

text.p: The White House said on Tuesday that it would be "in some sense, a declaration of economic war" for the United States to deny China renewal of most-favoured- nation trade status.

Its toughly-worded comment came in response to House Democratic leader Richard Gephardt's plan to fight President Bill Clinton on the China trade policy issue. Gephardt was to announce his position in a speech in Detroit later on Tuesday.

"Well, we'll charitably disagree," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said in reaction to the announcement. "The suspension of normal trade relations with China would be, in some sense, a declaration of economic war on China and would further isolate China from the world community."
McCurry was speaking in Paris, where the U.S. president earlier signed a pact between NATO and Russia on European security.

Clinton announced last week, ahead of a June 3 deadline, that he had decided to renew China's most-favoured-nation trade status, a designation that lets the world's most populous country continue to export goods to the United States at the tariff rate given most countries.

Every year since the 1989 Chinese army crackdown on pro- democracy demonstrators in Tiananmen Square, there have been unsuccessful congressional efforts to block MFN renewal. This year, however, Clinton faces an especially tough fight because of legislative concerns about an array of issues, including human rights in China, Beijing's takeover of Hong Kong and alleged Chinese efforts to buy U.S. influence by funnelling money to political candidates.

"It's long been our policy view that engagement with China is more likely to produce the changes in behaviour that the American people seek. And isolation is likely to produce exactly the opposite reaction," McCurry said.
Gephardt's defection on the China MFN issue was the second time that the party leader has broken ranks with the Democratic president on an important policy issue.

The Missouri lawmaker, a prospective rival to Vice President Al Gore for the Democratic presidential nomination in the year 2000, last week came out against the balanced budget agreement that Clinton negotiated with leaders of the Republican majority in Congress.
